name: The Replacements
label: Twin/Tone
lede: A janitor with a notebook walks in on two teenage brothers and a drummer in a Minneapolis basement, and over twelve years they write Let It Be and Pleased to Meet Me and just as dependably wreck the shows meant to sell them.

eras.title: A janitor hears the basement through the wall
eras.text: The Stinson brothers and Chris Mars start as a cover band with no singer. Paul Westerberg joins, Peter Jesperson hears a tape, and a church hall ban hands them a new name.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Replacements (band) · Wikipedia: Tommy Stinson
years.h: Bob Stinson gives his kid brother a bass, and Dogbreath has a rhythm section
years.p: [[Bob Stinson|49771251-1082-4a3d-b48f-ba39e3be4a2b]] hands eleven-year-old [[Tommy Stinson|3182bda5-2f4a-49e4-9fa3-cf7e5ebbff24]] a bass and recruits drummer [[Chris Mars|b0fefe3c-b393-4498-9b33-255b02d75716]]. With no singer, they cover Aerosmith, Ted Nugent and Yes.
years.xp:
Wikipedia puts the band's formation at 1979 but dates its beginnings to 1978, when Bob gave Tommy the bass. The trio rehearsed in the Stinson family house in south Minneapolis.

The set was arena rock, and nobody was out front. That changes next year.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Replacements (band) · St. Louis Magazine
years.h: A janitor cleaning a senator's office hears the Stinsons rehearse
years.p: [[Paul Westerberg|d558f844-4db0-4bc3-ba22-49ad2ca2722e]] is working in U.S. Senator David Durenberger's office when he hears them. Mars invites him to jam, and he ends up replacing the singer.
years.xp:
According to Wikipedia, Westerberg got the job by telling the outgoing vocalist "The band doesn't like you."

St. Louis Magazine, summarizing Bob Mehr's biography Trouble Boys, says the band came to the janitor as high school dropouts, and that Bob would punch Tommy in the face when he made mistakes.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Replacements (band) · Wikipedia: Twin/Tone Records
years.h: Westerberg hands a four-song basement demo to a record store clerk
years.p: [[Peter Jesperson|00cefb4a-65c2-4faa-812a-8f182b5bc8e9]] runs the Oar Folkjokeopus record store and co-runs Twin/Tone Records. He plays the tape at the counter and signs the band that year.
years.xp:
Jesperson later described the moment: "I didn't even get through the first song before I thought my head was going to explode."

Twin/Tone was founded in 1977 by Jesperson, Charley Hallman and Paul Stark. It released more than 300 records before closing in 1994.

years.h: A church hall bans the Impediments, and they come back as the Replacements
years.p: After a drunken show they played without Tommy, the band was thrown out for disorderly conduct. Wikipedia says the ban is what led them to rename themselves.
years.xp: The band had just discovered the Clash and the Damned and dropped the Dogbreath repertoire. They had renamed themselves the Impediments, and the ban came under that name.

years.cap: Westerberg, Mars, Tommy Stinson and Bob Stinson in an early Twin/Tone promo photo
years.h: At Jay's Longhorn, the Replacements play their first show under that name
years.p: A Minneapolis punk bar hosts the debut. Westerberg fronts, Tommy Stinson is still a teenager, and there is no record yet.

eras.title: Three records and a talent for getting thrown out
eras.text: Sorry Ma, Stink and Hootenanny come out on Twin/Tone, the band tours the country for the first time, and New York does not warm to them.

yt: Live at the 7th Street Entry, set one (1981)
years.h: Sorry Ma, Forgot to Take Out the Trash arrives on Twin/Tone
years.p: Recorded in July 1980 and again from March to June 1981, released August 25. The first single, "I'm in Trouble," came out August 7.
years.xp:
Westerberg, Jesperson and Steve Fjelstad produced. "Somethin to Dü" is the band's nod to fellow Twin Cities punks [[Hüsker Dü|5c4c90a4-539f-4101-83cf-301bc6a94e06]].

Robert Christgau gave it a B+ in the Village Voice. AllMusic's Stephen Thomas Erlewine later placed it among the strongest LPs the scene produced in the early '80s.
play: Sorry Ma, Forgot to Take Out the Trash

years.h: Stink opens on a recording of police breaking up a rent party
years.p: Eight songs in 14 minutes 24 seconds, recorded at Blackberry Way in one session on March 13 and released June 24. The first track is "Kids Don't Follow."
years.xp:
The audio comes from a January 29, 1982 raid on a rent party at the Harmony Building in Minneapolis.

Jesperson and Fjelstad produced. Wikipedia describes it as the band's hardcore punk attempt.

years.h: Hootenanny swaps instruments and keeps going
years.p: Released April 29. Westerberg is alone on "Within Your Reach"; on the title track Mars plays lead guitar and Bob Stinson plays bass.
years.xp:
Recording ran from October 1982 to January 1983, mostly at the Stark/Mudge Mobile Unit warehouse in Brooklyn Center, with sessions at Blackberry Way and a basement.

"Lovelines" takes its words from the City Pages classifieds, and the cover was drawn by Hüsker Dü's [[Grant Hart|571e1aad-0512-45ec-a26d-1d09d786cc53]], credited as Fake Name Graphx. Wikipedia reports over 38,000 vinyl copies sold.

years.cap: The four original Replacements in a 1983 Twin/Tone publicity portrait
years.h: Tommy Stinson leaves tenth grade for the first U.S. tour
years.p: The band hits the road in April 1983 with a roadie named Bill Sullivan.

years.h: CBGB throws out Bob Stinson on arrival, then books them last of five
years.p: The band reaches New York in June 1983 and plays early Monday morning to a room that has mostly left.
years.xp:
Wikipedia says shows at CBGB and Folk City that trip did badly because the band was so loud.

Later that summer they opened eight dates for R.E.M. Per the same account, the band decided to alienate the audience and several members threatened to quit.

eras.title: Let It Be, and Sire takes notice
eras.text: The 1984 record is the first one that makes the case for Westerberg as a songwriter. A live tape shows what the labels were watching, and Sire signs them anyway.

years.cap: The Replacements in a 1984 band portrait, the year of Let It Be
years.src: Wikipedia: Let It Be · Wikipedia: The Replacements (band)
years.h: Let It Be gets its cover on the roof of the Stinsons' mother's house
years.p: Recorded at Blackberry Way from August 1983 to February 1984 and released October 2. Robert Christgau gave it an A+.
years.xp:
The cover photo, by Daniel Corrigan, was taken on that roof. The current owners of the house added a stained-glass window of it in 2019.

Westerberg said "playing that kind of noisy, fake hardcore rock was getting us nowhere," and called it the first time he had songs the band arranged.

[[Peter Buck|2bab20bf-8dab-4af8-b7b0-ba8e30860261]] of R.E.M. was rumored to be producing. He says he did pre-production, one solo (on "I Will Dare"), and gave them some ideas. Steve Fjelstad and Jesperson produced. Rolling Stone later ranked it #15 among the albums of the 1980s.

years.cap: Live at the 7th Street Entry, Minneapolis
years.src: Wikipedia: The Replacements (band) · Wikipedia: For Sale
years.h: The Shit Hits the Fans is a live tape with the false starts left in
years.p: The cassette is the band's only live release for decades. Wikipedia describes it as an example of the intentionally poor shows label reps got to see.
years.xp:
By 1985 several major labels were interested. Wikipedia says the band was broke and Bob Stinson was working as a pizza chef.

Tommy Stinson said in 2007 that there were no good Replacements live recordings.

years.h: Tim is the Sire debut, produced by the Ramones' original drummer
years.p: Recorded June to July 1985 at Nicollet Studios, released September 18 per Wikipedia. The producer was Tommy Erdelyi, known as Tommy Ramone.
years.xp:
Sire's Seymour Stein signed the band; he had managed the Ramones. The "Bastards of Young" video is a single shot of a speaker.

Wikipedia lists the peak at #183 on the Billboard 200. Rolling Stone's review said the record's swagger and unpolished reflection became a template for grunge, alt-country and later emo.

The band page on Wikipedia dates the release to October 1985, and the album page to September 18.

eras.title: A Hoboken tape, a banned TV spot, a missing guitarist
eras.text: Six months on a major label produce the most famous bad night on television, a Maxwell's set that sits in the can for 31 years, and the end of the original four.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Replacements (band) · St. Louis Magazine
yt: Kiss Me on the Bus, Old Grey Whistle Test (not SNL)
years.h: They show up drunk on Saturday Night Live and get banned
years.p: Last-minute guests, they play "Bastards of Young" out of tune, then return wearing each other's clothes for "Kiss Me on the Bus." Lorne Michaels bans them.
years.xp:
Wikipedia says [[G.E. Smith|a289a494-cd2d-458b-91b8-f161dd467626]], SNL's music director and a fan, arranged the booking. He told the story that crew members had smuggled liquor into the dressing room and Bob Stinson fell in the corridor and broke his guitar, so SNL lent him one.

Wikipedia also notes Westerberg is heard swearing off-microphone at Bob. Per Trouble Boys, as summarized by St. Louis Magazine, Michaels said they would never work in television again. Westerberg came back as a solo act in 1993.

yt: Bastards of Young, live at Maxwell's 1986
years.h: Sire books a mobile studio for Maxwell's, Hoboken, and shelves the tape
years.p: Seymour Stein wanted a recording to use as a marketing tool. It came out 31 years later.
years.xp:
For Sale: Live at Maxwell's 1986 came out on Rhino on October 6, 2017, produced by Bob Mehr. It reached #52 on the Billboard 200, and Pitchfork gave it an 8.7.

Wikipedia notes it captures the band months before Bob Stinson was gone.

years.cap: Paul Westerberg on stage in Toronto, April 6, 1986
years.src: Wikipedia: Bob Stinson · Wikipedia: The Replacements (band) · Life of the Record
years.h: Bob Stinson leaves the band he started
years.p: Wikipedia says he was fired or chose to leave, or both, over creative and personal differences and his drinking and drug use. Westerberg said he ran out of ideas that Bob could shine on.
years.xp:
Bob Stinson's Wikipedia page says he was forced out in summer 1986 and that the band later reframed it as growing up. Westerberg is quoted: "we drank and took drugs a lot... But Bob thought that was the Replacements." The band page dates it to August 1986; Tommy Stinson's page says 1985.

Manager Peter Jesperson was fired the same year. He said it was like being thrown out of a club he had helped start.

Life of the Record has Westerberg saying they were thinking of breaking up the band when they let Bob go, and instead kept the trio.

eras.title: Memphis, a new guitarist, a roadie encore
eras.text: Pleased to Meet Me is made by a trio, Slim Dunlap takes the guitar, and two attempts at radio follow. It ends in a Chicago park with the roadies on stage.

years.cap: On stage at the Pier in Raleigh, 1987
years.src: Wikipedia: Pleased to Meet Me · Life of the Record
years.h: Three Replacements go to Memphis and make Pleased to Meet Me
years.p: Recorded at Ardent Studios from November 1986 to January 1987 with producer Jim Dickinson. It is the only Replacements studio album made as a trio.
years.xp:
Westerberg met Alex Chilton at a 1984 CBGB show, per Life of the Record, and the song "Alex Chilton" grew from that awkward first meeting. Chilton and the Memphis Horns played on the record. Bob Stinson turned up for one session, and Dickinson's joke working title was "Where's Bob?"

Luther Dickinson recalls his father putting a toxic waste barrel in front of Mars's kick drum for a "polluted sound." Westerberg said going to Memphis was the coolest thing they ever did.

It placed third in the Village Voice's 1987 Pazz & Jop poll.

years.src: Life of the Record · Wikipedia: Pleased to Meet Me
years.h: Warner Bros. flies 30 to 40 industry people to Memphis and picks up the option
years.p: The playback party for Pleased to Meet Me ends with the label exercising the band's contract option on the spot. Westerberg's verdict, per Bob Mehr:
years.xp:
Life of the Record reports the album about doubled Tim's sales, to roughly 250,000 copies, which was a disappointment at the time.

The Wikipedia album page cites journalist Michael Azerrad for about 300,000.

years.h: First Avenue's janitor, Slim Dunlap, takes the guitar job
years.p: [[Slim Dunlap|0e10e22b-2a2f-48f8-b54f-cc1523312dce]] turns Westerberg down at first. He joins in 1987 out of admiration for the songs and stays until the end.
years.xp:
He was working as a janitor at First Avenue, the club where the band started. Wikipedia quotes him preferring to "just play guitar and let the other guy lose all the money."

His first solo record, The Old New Me, came out in 1993, made for under $10,000.

years.h: Don't Tell a Soul goes after radio, and "I'll Be You" gets there
years.p: Released February 1 on Sire. Recorded at Cherokee Studios in Hollywood with producer Matt Wallace and mixed by Chris Lord-Alge.
years.xp:
"I'll Be You" is the band's only Hot 100 entry. It hit #51 on May 13, 1989 and also topped the Modern Rock chart.

Westerberg was not sold on the polish: "I thought the little things I'd cut in my basement were closer to what I wanted." Wallace's remix of the album came out in 2019 as Dead Man's Pop.

years.h: All Shook Down starts as a Westerberg solo record
years.p: Management talked him into releasing it as the Replacements. John Cale plays viola on "Sadly Beautiful" and Johnette Napolitano sings on "My Little Problem."
years.xp:
Wikipedia notes there are no clear records of who played on which tracks. Rolling Stone ranked it third among its 1990 albums of the year.

Chris Mars left in November 1990, and his last appearance as a Replacement was in the "Merry Go Round" video. Steve Foley replaced him for the tour.

years.h: Chris Mars quits after All Shook Down, and Steve Foley takes the drums
years.p: Mars had drummed since the Dogbreath days. Foley plays the final six months.

years.h: In Chicago, the roadies play the encore, and then nothing for 22 years
years.p: At Taste of Chicago, with Material Issue, each band member wanders off during the set and a roadie takes his place. Fans call it "It Ain't Over 'Til the Fat Roadie Plays."
years.xp:
WXRT in Chicago broadcast the show live. It was the last time the band played until Riot Fest in 2013.

Their last tour, with Elvis Costello, had ended at Madison Square Garden in June. Wikipedia describes the band as having disbanded in 1991.

eras.title: Afterward
eras.text: Bob Stinson dies in 1995, Tommy Stinson ends up in Guns N' Roses, Steve Foley dies in 2008, and Slim Dunlap has a stroke in 2012.

years.h: Bob Stinson dies at 35
years.p: He was found in his Uptown Minneapolis apartment. Two weeks later the Hennepin County medical examiner gave the cause as organ failure from years of drug and alcohol abuse.
years.xp:
Early press speculated about an overdose, and a syringe was found next to him. Wikipedia and Bob Mehr both report the medical examiner ruled that out. An assistant medical examiner said, "There is such a thing as total body failure."

His mother Anita bought a park bench near the Lake of the Isles in Minneapolis in his memory. Recordings from his last band, the Bleeding Hearts, came out in 2022 as Riches to Rags.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Replacements (band) · Wikipedia: Tommy Stinson
years.h: Tommy Stinson takes Duff McKagan's place in Guns N' Roses
years.p: After [[Bash & Pop|c44092a6-d6be-4bfa-9650-edccc69f7a2b]] and Perfect, he joins [[Guns N' Roses|eeb1195b-f213-4ce1-b28c-8565211f8e43]] in 1998 on drummer Josh Freese's recommendation, at 31, and stays until McKagan comes back.
years.xp:
He also toured and recorded with [[Soul Asylum|b10db9ad-b4c3-47f3-a7a4-37864b134f65]] from 2005 to 2011 and put out solo records, Village Gorilla Head in 2004 and One Man Mutiny in 2011.

Westerberg released Folker in 2004, a return to melodic lo-fi, and Chris Mars settled into a career as a visual artist.

years.h: Rhino adds two new songs, with Josh Freese on drums, to a compilation
years.p: Don't You Know Who I Think I Was? pairs Twin/Tone and Sire tracks with "Pool & Dive" and "Message to the Boys," cut by Westerberg, Stinson and Mars at Flowers Studio in Minneapolis.
years.xp:
Rhino followed with deluxe editions of the four Twin/Tone albums on April 22, 2008 and the Sire albums on September 24, 2008.

Wikipedia lists the session as a one-off, not a reunion.

years.h: Steve Foley, who drummed the last tour, dies
years.p: Wikipedia reports an accidental overdose of prescription medication.

years.cap: The reunion set at Riot Fest, Chicago
years.src: Wikipedia: The Replacements (band) · Wikipedia: Slim Dunlap · Wikipedia: Peter Jesperson
years.h: Friends rally around Slim Dunlap after his stroke
years.p: Wikipedia says Dunlap had a severe stroke in February 2012. Peter Jesperson organizes Songs for Slim, and Westerberg and Tommy Stinson record a 10-inch for it.
years.xp:
The Songs for Slim EP, in a 250-copy vinyl edition, was auctioned online for Dunlap's medical costs. Jesperson's Wikipedia page calls it the closest thing yet to a Replacements reunion.

A live album, Thank You Dancers!, followed in 2020.

years.src: Slicing Up Eyeballs · Wikipedia: The Replacements
years.h: Color Me Obsessed hands the story to the fans
years.p: Gorman Bechard's documentary has almost no Replacements playing on screen. Noisey and Vice streamed it on YouTube in December.
years.xp: Slicing Up Eyeballs described it as a two-hour documentary about the Replacements and their rabid fans, streamed for a limited time.

eras.title: Twenty-two years later
eras.text: Westerberg and Tommy Stinson come back with Dave Minehan on guitar and Josh Freese on drums. Three summers on, they are done.

years.cap: The reunion set at Riot Fest Toronto, Fort York, August 25, 2013
years.h: Riot Fest Toronto brings them back after 22 years
years.p: A 23-song, 75-minute set at Fort York, with Dave Minehan on guitar and Josh Freese on drums. Rolling Stone says nearly 10,000 people rushed the stage for "Can't Hardly Wait."
years.xp:
Westerberg opened by apologizing that it took so long, and said they had been having a wardrobe debate that was unresolved. He forgot some words and the crowd filled them in.

The set opened with the first track from Sorry Ma and ended on a song inspired by an Iggy Pop autograph. More Riot Fest dates followed in Chicago and Denver.

years.cap: Westerberg and Tommy Stinson at Riot Fest Chicago
years.h: Billie Joe Armstrong sits in at Coachella
years.p: The Replacements play two sets, April 11 and 18, and [[Billie Joe Armstrong|5d06fe54-485a-4a07-b506-5f6f719448cb]] of Green Day joins on the second date.

years.h: Twenty-eight years after SNL, they play network TV again
years.p: The song on The Tonight Show is "Alex Chilton."

years.big: "I have always loved you. Now I must whore my past."
q: I have always loved you. Now I must whore my past.
years.h: Westerberg tells Primavera Sound it's the last show
years.p: At Primavera Sound in Porto, days after a Spain date, he announces on stage that this is the band's final performance. The T-shirts had said it first.
years.xp:
Wikipedia says the message was split over two shirts, one letter on each side. In February 2015 co-manager Darren Hill said the band had laid down seven or eight songs for a possible album.

Tommy Stinson said that September they had dipped their toe in the water, and it did not feel so good.

eras.title: The book, and a death
eras.text: Bob Mehr's biography tells the whole story in 2016. Slim Dunlap dies in 2024.

years.cap: Tommy Stinson solo at Frank's in San Antonio, October 9, 2016
years.h: Bob Mehr's Trouble Boys lays out the whole story
years.p: Mehr's biography, written with band access, covers the Stinson brothers, the drinking, Bob's death from organ failure, and the way the group sabotaged its own shot at fame.
years.xp:
In a March 2016 NPR interview, Mehr described them as legends who never quite became stars.

He also produced the live Maxwell's album.

years.h: Slim Dunlap dies at 73
years.p: His family said the cause was complications from the 2012 stroke. He died at his Minneapolis home.
